utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Before we continue shall we have a word about the scheduling issue. Where are we? Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. We are asking to be able to call some of the regularly scheduled witnesses for next week before we have the next expert on this Mile Poparic. And as I understand it, the problem from the Prosecution's point of view is that Mr. Gaynor is here specially for those two witnesses and it would delay his return. We tried -- we contacted the witnesses for next week who had previously been scheduled on other occasions and they were really unable to change their plans and told us -- two of them told us that they would not be willing to testify if we once again had to reschedule them. So we feel that on balance the risk of losing the witnesses is too great to overcome our desire to try to help the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: How about the third one?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The third one has -- this is his second time scheduled but we haven't been able to reach him to determine what his reaction would be if we have to postpone his testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the total amount of time for his -- for their evidence in chief and cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, you haven't given us the cross-examination times, but the chief for each of them is half an hour or less.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I think parties have been informed about the amount of time for the cross-examinations. Could you give the names?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We can discuss it in public session?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we can. It's Vladimir Lukic and Dane Katanic and Svetozar Kosoric.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Lukic who used to be an interpreter?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No, he was the prime minister.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: The interpreter, Petar Uscumlic, has also been fixed to testify Tuesday morning but his testimony is one-quarter hour on direct and one-quarter hour on cross, and I don't think the Prosecution has any problem with us proceeding with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: If Chambers staff could approach the bench.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, do you have anything to add, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't know if it assists the Court in the cross-examination time issue, but it may refresh the Court's recollection, if I'm accurate, that this was an unusually long statement, nearly -- I think nearly a hundred pages and -- hundred paragraphs, excuse me. And relatively equal number of documents if I recall so it was pretty voluminous, and I don't know if that refreshes the Court's recollection. The only thing that I would --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What do you mean by this. Ms. Subotic's evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: No, Mr. Lukic. You were asking about him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Lukic, oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: And I -- the only thing I would add is that I understand that the -- I understand the discussion we've been having with respect at least to Mr. Lukic and Mr. Katanic, but I understand that both -- there wasn't any concerted effort to get ahold of Mr. Kosoric and what's more I understand he's a retiree in not far distant from here. So I think the likelihood of that being a particular inconvenience for him is pretty remote. So I don't think he falls at least in the same category for purposes of Mr. Robinson's argument as the other witnesses. The Court is aware of our argument -- of our position, and basically I'd simply say that we -- that this is not -- although we acknowledge, by the way, the accommodations that the Defence in the past and I trust that they acknowledge the many accommodations and acts of co-operation and indeed direct assistance from the Prosecution which has overall been I think an excellent working relationship, that this is not that kind of situation. As I noted in my e-mail to the Court, this is a situation where there was an agreement where -- where arrangements were made, built around that agreement, and it -- the problems arise from the decision by the Defence to use their time in a particular way without notifying anyone in advance that that was going to be done. So that's the simplest version or recap of the position we find ourselves in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the Chamber's at a loss when there's disagreement between the parties, in particular as far as it's related to the order of witnesses. The Chamber cannot leave it to the presenting party. But I wonder whether having some extended hours would resolve the issue?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, that's one thing about which there appears to be a consensus at the moment and that is I noted in Mr. Robinson's e-mail that he didn't feel that it would successfully resolve the impasse and having looked at the schedule and consulted with the attorneys involved I agree. I -- we considered before that that might be a way of sort of avoiding or getting around the impasse, but it doesn't seem to be. So I wouldn't prevail upon the Court for extended hours, given the -- what appears to be the negligible impact on this particular scheduling issue.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: And next week we are sitting only for three days?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So if you could, both of you, have a word during the break and come back to the Chamber as to what extent we need to extend the sitting hours, in what terms. And in the meantime I'll ask around the staff and interpreters, court reporters, et cetera, as to its feasibility and its extent. Shall we continue then? Yes, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours. And if we could have on the screen D3542, page 91 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Good morning, Ms. Subotic.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [In English] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm going to ask you now about -- we're still on scheduled incident G5. I have a couple more questions about that incident. And I'd like to ask you about paragraph 60(f), which is on page 91 in the B/C/S and page 43 in the English. Now, the figure you've included - if we could make the photo in the middle of the screen a bit bigger - this is a still from a video taken at the scene of the incident shortly after it occurred. And at paragraph 60(f) you note that Mr. Cavcic the ballistics investigator examined and took into account damage caused by shell fragments to the rear of this Skoda vehicle. And you assert that an extract from the film that was recorded after the explosion, and that is V0002479 at two hours and 17 seconds to two hours and 23 seconds. It's footnoted at number -- footnote number 216. You state that: "This video extract clearly shows the areas penetrated by the shell fragments on the bumper of the Skoda car." And you claim that you have been able to determine the direction from which the fragments entered the car and you have marked that direction with the yellow arrows on this video still. Now, what I'd like to do now is play the portion of the video that you've relied on here that's referenced in footnote 216. If you could just watch that video, it's just a few seconds. And this is, sorry, 65 ter 40621A.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And if -- since it's very short, if we could just watch it one more time.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Subotic, if you could just confirm that this is indeed the video footage that in your opinion allows you to establish the direction from which the shell fragments penetrated the car, and I'm quoting from your report now: "Corroborate with greatest clarity and unambiguity the previous findings that the shell had come in from the north, or rather, the north-east." This is the portion of the video you rely on for those assertions; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, you're right.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Subotic, I'm going to suggest to you that your conclusions are absolutely impossible to draw on the basis of what we just saw. You can barely see any shrapnel damage at all, let alone determine the direction those fragments entered the car. Would you like to respond to that?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're obviously looking at -- I can't see the transcript, so I don't know if I'm fast. You're obviously looking at this footage partially. The footage was viewed in the context of the overall evidence retrieved on the site, the ones that we looked at yesterday, and based on the descriptions provided by the Bosnian investigators in their findings. Therefore, this image clearly indicates that following the explosion of the shell, the shrapnel came in from top to the bottom, from the left to the right, as we look at the image, which is consistent with the explosion site which we determined and is consistent with the incoming trajectory. If you recall I did describe the process of fragmentation the other day. Therefore, the shape of the damage inflicted on the bumper clearly determined the direction of fire which in turn determines the incoming trajectory of the shell. This is perhaps how it should have been formulated in order to make it completely clear. In other words, this photograph wasn't or this still wasn't viewed in isolation without regard of all the other -- without regard to all the other evidence, quite the inverse, it was regarded in the context.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Please when you'd like to intervene, please wait, do not overlap. Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Sorry. I don't think it's identical. I think few frames earlier -- should be stopped few frames earlier.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We know that but --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But if this extract is slightly longer than the one the witness referred to, I don't see a problem, if I understand what the accused is saying correctly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yeah, if we compare the figure 50 with this still, we can notice that there's no difficulty with proceeding at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And just to be clear, what I was playing was the portion of the video footnoted in the report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In their entirety.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And I tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it's not in evidence?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you give us the time-frame or you're going to tender excerpt of this part only?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We'll admit it.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: As Exhibit P6320, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. To avoid any confusion, the frame which was shown in the report is the one immediately preceding the one we have on our screens. Just to make sure that there is no confusion about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. I confirmed that.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, if we could go to paragraph 60(g) of your report which is at page 43 of the English and page 91 of the B/C/S. Again that's D3542.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we are on that page.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is where you discuss the position that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could we switch to e-court.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry, and if we could go to page 92 of the B/C/S where we see the picture -- photograph in question. And this, Ms. Subotic, is where you discuss the position that the stabiliser was found in after this incident. And you claim at paragraph 60(g) that the stabiliser could not have ended up there if the shell had come in from the west or the north-west. And I note you make a similar type of claim with respect to the Markale 2 incident, where the stabiliser was kicked back - and that was at pages 44 and 45 of yesterday's transcript - where you say that the stabiliser couldn't have ended up in the position lateral to the explosion site that it was found in. Now, for this incident, for G5, it's common ground that the shell exploded somewhere above the surface, and therefore the stabiliser was freed from the shell casing somewhere above the surface. But you don't know, do you, whether the stabiliser continued to move forward or whether it was kicked back because you don't know the velocity of the shell or the charge that it was fired from; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your question is rather complex so I have to provide you with a more comprehensive answer. It is true that we don't know either the velocity at which the shell flew in nor do we know which charge was used to launch the projectile. However, had the shell been fired with the fourth charge and above, the stabiliser would definitely continue flying along its incoming trajectory or let's maybe be quite precise, along the trajectory approximate to the incoming trajectory of the shell and would then have become embedded in the ground. Now, since it was not embedded in the ground, it either had to fall into a spot that would be close to the site of explosion or it would have had to be propelled back along its incoming trajectory. But obviously it did not end up embedded in the ground, rather, it fell.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But, Ms. Subotic, that rule that you say about when a stabiliser would become embedded in the ground only applies when the shell hits the surface. In this case the shell hit a person. So even if it had a charge sufficient to let it continue to travel, it would be travelling through a person and wouldn't necessarily get embedded in the ground because there would be a obstacle, namely, the person that the shell impacted. So you can't draw any conclusions about the fact that the stabiliser was not embedded in this instance because the shell didn't strike the surface of the ground; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Obviously you misunderstood what I was saying the other day. The process of separation of the stabiliser ensues after the explosion. So the explosion occurs first. The activation occurred on the body of the person. The person was struck and suffered its destruction as a result of the fragmentation effect and blast effect or the shock wave effect. All of this happened practically at the same time as the stabiliser was propelled back from the body. So that is a rule that is in force or is valid whenever an explosion occurs, regardless of what the -- of what surface is involved. It is part and parcel of the process of the activation of the shell itself. Either you misunderstood me yesterday or I wasn't precise enough. Therefore, this rule is valid in every case, regardless of the reason why the shell is activated. This is the physicality that accompanies the process of the activation of the shell and its destruction. At any rate, it should not penetrate the person because the person would be struck and knocked down by the shock wave effect. This is a process that isn't simultaneous, you know, it's sequential. What occurs on the body of a person as injury happens independently. The stabiliser has its own velocity and we have its action against a person that is static or stationary at that point and we have of course also the velocity that would occur after it is being propelled back. I don't know if I understand clearly what you were saying or if you've understood me clearly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I think I understand --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. This is the pace we should proceed in. French translation has just been completed. Please continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I think I understand it's your position here that the stabiliser was kicked back, and in such a circumstance the -- do I misunderstood you?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So the stabiliser was kicked back and ultimately --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes to what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Had -- that I answered that at the point of destruction the stabiliser was kicked back along its incoming trajectory, of course in the opposite direction --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the witness repeat what she just said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me add one other thing. None of us present here, including the investigators, can claim that the stabiliser dropped exactly in this spot. When the stabiliser falls, it can have a ricochet and then fall elsewhere. Of course it wouldn't be too far from its first point of contact with the ground. We had that at Dobrinja when we were looking at that stabiliser which had some sort of deformation on the fins of the stabiliser and it was not in contact with the surface. And of course we knew that it had to have been in contact with the surface since it had those deformations. At any rate, this stabiliser did not become embedded and cannot serve as the incoming trajectory. Had the shell really flown in along the trajectory determined by the investigators, it would not -- one would not be able to find it there at all.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Ms. Subotic, I'm going to ask you to try to keep your answers as concise as possible because my time is very limited. So you agree that the stabiliser was -- or it's your position the stabiliser was kicked back. In such a circumstance, the stabiliser, as you point out, could have ricochetted off something and then bounced back in an unknown -- bounced off an object in an unknown direction. Similarly, in the immediate aftermath of the incident --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Firstly, due to something missing in the transcript, Ms. Gustafson may be misguided. Dr. Subotic said "a bit to the left at a specific point" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Can the accused please repeat the reference.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And then what is noted in the question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. If you could repeat, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Firstly, on page 11 in line 12, what is missing is that Dr. Subotic said "and somewhat to the left that it bounced off to the opposite direction from the incoming trajectory and somewhat to the left." And in line 9 in the question that she said "unknown direction," she did not say "unknown direction," but she said that it was along the incoming trajectory but in the opposite direction and somewhat to the left. So if we can clarify this, please, because if the question is wrong then everything goes astray.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you confirm having said so?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Subotic, not only could the stabiliser easily have ricochetted off an object and then been deflected in an unknown direction, but in the immediate aftermath of this incident as well as the Markale incident, as people are rushing around in total chaos and terror trying to help horribly injured people, it's quite probable that someone would have accidentally moved the stabiliser by kicking it or dragging a body over it or any number of possible scenarios. You simply can't draw any conclusions from the ultimate position that the stabiliser was found in after the incident, can you?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Generally speaking, you are right. However, the stabiliser is located immediately next to the wheel, and if it landed there and had not been kicked there, then the likelihood that someone moved it from there in some sort of manipulation is very small. That's one detail. Another detail is the following: The paragraph just like the previous is not something where this is observed separately apart from other markings on the ground. So when we say this, it means just the following: Judging by the position of the body, the traces on the bumper, the traces on the asphalt, and the entire appearance of the crime scene and the direction of the stabiliser itself, that was all used to determine the incoming trajectory. And everything fits in. The markings on the bumper, the position of the body, the position of the stabiliser, and the entire appearance seems to confirm the incoming trajectory which we established. I mean, we did not consider any of these elements separately as conclusive evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to now move on to G4, which is the shelling in Dobrinja of the football-match.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Could you read out the last sentence on this page which appears after (h). Could you read aloud.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "During the visit of the crime scene, the Defence team in September 2010 found markings on the asphalt made by fragments of the shell, figure 52. "These markings show unequivocally that the shell" --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The next sentence.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The one that begins with the words "these marks"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "These marks show unequivocally that the shell had come in from the north and that the claim that the shell had come in from the west or north-west is completely unfounded." What is meant here, the reference is to the claim made by the CSB.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So the proposition for this statement is that the -- if the stabiliser landed on that exactly the same place as was marked and not moved from the original place? Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have not understood what you just said. Are you correct in concluding ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Because you said in -- previously, previously -- generally speaking Ms. Gustafson "was right. However, the stabiliser is located immediately next to the wheel and if it landed there and had not been kicked there, then the likelihood that someone moved it from there in some sort of manipulation is very small." So your conclusion in this sentence is predicated that it was not moved at all. Am I correct in so understanding?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It can be concluded from this that it was not moved for the reason that it fits into the whole appearance provided by the physical traces found on the site and not because we disregarded such a possibility. But you drew an appropriate conclusion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd like to ask you now about incident G4. If we could go to page 73 in the B/C/S, where there's a figure I'd like you to look at first. And the reference in the English is page 29. And if we could zoom in a bit on the map on the left-hand side. And if we could make it a bit bigger, maybe collapse the English. Now, Ms. Subotic, you'll recognise this. This is where you've identified the location of the incident and the front lines and done some measurements and you conclude that the front line in generally the east or south-easterly direction is about 270 metres from the incident. And you would agree -- would you agree on the basis of this map and your calculations that if it had been the ABiH or if this shell had been fired from ABiH territory to the south-east of this incident location, that it would have to have been fired from a very close distance, from approximately 200 metres away. Would you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We -- aha. Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If I can help you a bit. You can see the front line follows the road that is just to the south-east of some apartment blocks. So the only place the shell could have been fired from is the -- to the -- on the other side of those apartment blocks in ABiH territory which would be roughly 200 metres from the incident site. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can agree with that, but then it did not have to be launched from there. I mean, we investigated where it was launched from on the basis of physical traces. We determined the trajectory and everything else.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, and the trajectory you concluded was this south-easterly trajectory. So I'm saying that if it was fired from that trajectory, from ABiH territory, the furthest distance it could have been fired from is 200 metres from the incident. Are we agreed on that?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And if we could go to 65 ter 25057 now, please. And what is about to come up on the screen, Ms. Subotic, is a Google Earth image of the same general location, but instead of coming from straight above, down, it's taken at a slight angle so you can see a little bit of the scene. It's also oriented so that it's basically the shot from more or less the north or north-east looking towards the south or south-west. Do you recognise this photo as depicting the same area that you've included in the map in figure 35, this area of Dobrinja relevant to this incident? And if you use the circular road or the oval-shaped road roughly in the middle of the page, that should help to orient you. Maybe I can help you a bit more. I'm going to suggest to you that the parking-lot where the football-match was played or at least in the area where it was played is the -- in the courtyard that's on the bottom right-hand corner of that oval-shaped road. And then the front line is the -- runs along the road that goes up and down the -- relatively wide road that goes up and down the photo on the left-hand side of the photo. Does that make sense to you now?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's easier for me to be sincere to use my own image and to use what I already studied and the information included in the report because this is somewhat differently oriented than what I took from the internet.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I ask something. If it's from Google why isn't the north marked here? Where is the north here?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Given the witness's answer, I'll just move on. I won't use this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: If we could now go to page 65 in the B/C/S and page 25 in the English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And this is relating to paragraph 37 of your report, Ms. Subotic, where you take issue with Mr. Houdet's, or Captain Houdet's crater analysis that he carried out shortly after this incident. And at paragraph 37 you allege that there are some imprecisions in his report that cast doubt on the accuracy of that report which is in evidence as P1053, page 11. And one of those doubts you have is relating to the location that he plotted for this incident, and in figure 30 you claim to have plotted his grid references that he recorded for the impact locations and concluded that this was over 200 metres away from the parking-lot. You're aware, right, that different maps use different grid systems and there are different grid systems out there from which you can use to plot locations on maps; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right. We took that into account and when we did we found ourselves at a position which is around 200 metres away from the incident site. We took everything into account. During our analysis we reached this place. This is a matter of the imprecision of the system, the maps and the co-ordinates and the grid. So regardless of our good will to take everything into account, considering everything that you just mentioned, we determined the location which is 200 metres away from the place that was claimed to have been the place where the football-match took place.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. And again, if you could try to keep your answers as concise as possible, that would be helpful. Well, the UN investigation report to which Mr. Houdet's analysis was attached states with respect to his analysis: "No maps to interpret the grid references mentioned were available." And that's P1053, page 8, paragraph 16. Now, you don't have information about which specific grid system Mr. Houdet used either, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as I know, there are two systems. We checked both and we could not find the grid reference that would correspond with the location of the parking-lot.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And what's the basis for your conclusion that there are only two grid systems in the world?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm aware of two grid systems which depend on the number of figures which you read when you do the analysis.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you also noted that Mr. Houdet described a macadam surface in his crater analysis report, and you assert that, in fact, there was no macadam surface anywhere in or around the parking-lot - and that's paragraph 37 - and this is based on your understanding of the term "macadam" as being "a road laid with crushed stones," and that's footnote 134. Now, this stems, this conclusion of yours stems from a confusion about the term "macadam," and that's a confusion that you actually know was resolved because you were in the courtroom when it was resolved during Mr. Higgs' testimony at transcript page 6013 when Dr. Karadzic was putting to Mr. Higgs the exact same alleged discrepancy between Mr. Houdet's report and the tarmac surface of the parking-lot. Judge Morrison explained to the accused that in English "macadam" is the same as "tarmac" and that's at transcript page 6013. So in spite of the fact that you were in court when this linguistic confusion was resolved, you're continuing to persist in your belief that what Captain Houdet was referring to when he referred to a macadam surface in the English language is something other than "tarmac." And you know that's incorrect; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Firstly, I was present in the courtroom and I did hear the explanation. The word "macadam" means precisely in all languages what I stated down there and the word got its meaning after its inventor Mr. Macadam, who is a Scotsman, and it means in all languages what I noted there. It's a different issue whether there's a secondary or a third meaning in a specific language. What I said is correct. You can find it in any encyclopedia, and it's called after Mr. Macadam who is a Scotsman and it means precisely what I noted there.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So you dispute Judge Morrison's definition of the term "macadam," a native English-speaking Judge in this Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not disputing his definition. I'm just saying that in any encyclopedia it is very clearly defined what the word "macadam" means, and it is called so after the man who introduced that or invented it in that particular profession and whose last name was Macadam. And I really do not want to meddle with professions and languages that I'm not sufficient and familiar with and that are not my primary profession. I just said that macadam means that in every language, but I do not dispute that there might be a second or a third meaning of the same word as noted by Judge Morrison.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. I'd like to move on now to paragraph 42 and this is at page 29 of the English and page 71 of the B/C/S. And this is where you discuss Captain Houdet's conclusions about the -- about the distance from which the shell was fired based on the minimum angle of descent, and you point out that this is a mistake because it is, in fact, the maximum angle of descent that determines the minimum distance from which the shell is fired. So that -- on that point I agree with you, that's common ground. Captain Houdet made a mistake because he looked at the minimum angle of descent and determined the minimum distance of firing on that basis, and that's wrong. He should have looked at the maximum angle of descent and determined the minimum firing distance on that basis. We agree. But then you go on to take issue with Mr. Higgs' conclusion in his report at P1437, page 8, where he says: "Using the distance to the confrontation lines and the standard pattern of the mortar crater in addition to the reference (c)," which is a reference in his report, "I agree with Houdet's conclusion number 3 and that I agree that the mortar rounds must have been fired from the Serb side of the confrontation lines." And you state that this conclusion by Mr. Higgs is a sign of bias because Mr. Higgs must have been aware of the error in Captain Houdet's report. Now, in his testimony in the Galic case Mr. Higgs expanded on the basis for his agreement with Captain Houdet that the rounds must have been fired from the Serb side. And he explained that Captain Houdet did fail to determine the range from the possible angle of descent of the shell and he noted that you would obviously get a shorter range if the angle of descent was larger. And that's at transcript page 12469. And at transcript page 12467 in Galic, Mr. Higgs testified that from his analysis of the overall shape of the crater, he determined that the round must have been -- come in at a -- what he called a normal angle of between 50 and 70 degrees. Now, it's true, is it not, that if the maximum angle -- if Mr. Higgs is correct about the maximum angle being 70 degrees, then even if the mortar was fired at the lowest charge, it would have to have been fired from SRK-held territory. In other words, at least more than the 200 metres away which you claimed was the -- which you agreed was the maximum distance that the shell could have been fired from ABiH territory. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Excuse me, this was quite long. I tried to follow what you said as closely as I could. You mentioned that Mr. Higgs changed his position; with reference to what I quoted; and you also said that he assessed the angle of descent and also that he provided some distances. Is that correct? Have I followed that appropriately? What you said was too long for me to be able to take everything into account and provide a concise answer. Somewhere along the way I had a problem continuing to follow what you said, I lost you. So I would ask you to ask me questions that I could immediately answer, please, because it's really complicated to follow such a long introductory presentation and then having me answer you shortly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Certainly. I can do that. Let me ask it this way. Mr. Higgs in his Galic testimony concluded when he looked at the crater that it must have come in at an angle of between -- an angle of descent of between 50 and 70 degrees. So my question for you is: If he was correct and, in fact, the maximum angle of descent was 70 degrees, it's true, is it not, that the mortar would have to have been fired from the SRK side of the confrontation line? Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will agree with you if I look at the tables because I really don't know this by heart, the angles of descent, and whether we provided them in this document or not. I have to have a look at the angles. I really don't know the tables off the top of my head.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, I'll bring up then the 65 ter 24216A. This is the firing table for the 82-millimetre mortar that you rely on in your analysis for this incident. And that's referenced at footnote 16 --

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that they will be in here as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: 164. We have the relevant pages of the firing table. I'll bring them up on the screen and you can look at them. Ms. Subotic, if you could look at the screen you'll see the firing table for the M69 and M69A mortar and this is the one that you reference for this incident. If we could go to page 7 of the English and page 4 of the B/C/S. Sorry, I had it backwards. Page 7 in the B/C/S, page 4 in the English. And on the B/C/S if we could enlarge the table slightly. Now, you see column 4, Ms. Subotic, is the angles -- the angle of descent in degrees. And you can see that at an angle of 69.54 degrees --

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no, column 4 -- column 4 is not the angle of descent but the angle of launch. The angle of descent can be found in column 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Are we looking at the correct English page?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. The -- only the column headings have been translated.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Why are you showing me this table, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise. It should be page 8 in the English. The English translation is correct except we don't have a page for the primary charge but the table headings match. You're right, Ms. Subotic, it was my mistake. It should be column 9, where the angle is referenced in mils rather than degrees. And --

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have an objection. I don't know why are you showing me this table. As far as I can understand, was that a round 82? Was that what the table was for? Very well then, go on, what would you like to ask me?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Well, unfortunately, I can't read the relevant numbers because the 0 is planted right over top of it so I'm going to have to move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Ms. Gustafson, was it page 88 or page 8?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In the B/C/S it's page 7.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: In English.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: In English it should be -- this page shows the column headings. We don't have a page translated with the primary charge, but it's the same column headings. So this page -- the English that appears here depicts the correct column headings [overlapping speakers].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BAIRD
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, it's e-court page 8 but it says page 88 in --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes, because this is a partial -- this is an extract from the table which is very lengthy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But the B/C/S page says it's page 85.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's right, Your Honour, because it's an extract because the firing table is a several-hundred-page document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But where does that page 88 come from?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I'm lost.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No, you see the bottom of English page, left -- top left -- bottom left says page 88 --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: -- where does it come from?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes. It comes from the B/C/S because this is the translation of the first charge which is why it has a 1 on it instead of a 0, so it's not the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we see the lower part.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: So the column headings are the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, but my question is simply: Where does this page 88 come from?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It comes from page 88 in the B/C/S which is page 8 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: We do not have page 88.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: We do have page 88 in the B/C/S --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: -- it's page 8 of this document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But B/C/S says it has 34 pages.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Right, because this is just an extract from the larger document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. I'll leave it at that. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Subotic, just one more topic I'd like to cover on this incident and this is at page 75 of the B/C/S of your report, D3542, if we could go back to that, and this is paragraph 46 and the English page is page 31.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Paragraph 46, right?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The annotations on these two pages are different in reference to 70 and 101 at the top. These two pages cannot be compared, they are incomparable.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: She's not dwelling on that anymore. Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Now, Ms. Subotic, here you challenge the determination that the azimuth of the crater measured during the 1995 investigation was 110 degrees on the basis that in your view the investigators placed the compass on the wrong slat and that is based on your analysis of this photograph. Now, just preliminarily, do you agree that the red stick in the middle of this photograph does depict the central axis of the crater and the trajectory of the shell in this case, putting aside what was measured at the time. Just, in your view do you agree that the stick marked with red accurately depicts the central axis?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to how the traces are marked in this photo with the white chalk and what can be gleaned from the photo, I would say yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. And just to be clear, it's your position that the investigators mistakenly measured what is in this photo from our perspective the slat on the right-hand side, which would have been for them the slat on the left-hand side. That's right, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The conclusion was not based on that. The conclusion was corroborated and it was from the mismatch between the traces that we found on the site when we visited it and when we measured the axis as well as the size of the crater and the trajectory based on the azimuth in that parking and this is just the corroboration for the difference. That difference of some 30 or so degrees arose from the fact that they noted as their findings what we can see in the photo, irrespective of the fact that they determined the position of the central axis correctly. However, they noted the position of the compass that you can see in the photo, and based on the difference between the traces on the site and what they provided in their findings, we concluded that they made a mistake, that their measurements are wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in your report you state: "The photograph clearly shows that the magnetic compass was set on the right-hand slat marking the border of the fragment marked instead of being set on the central slat." Now you're referring to the right-hand slat. Based on what we can see as we're looking at the photo it's your position that --

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It would be my right as I'm sitting and looking at the photo.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Can we go to P1699, page 7 of the B/C/S, please. And if we could zoom in on the top photograph. This is a photograph from the photo file that was taken at the time these measurements were made. It's taken looking down on the crater, obviously, and you can see the reddish stick depicting the central axis. The stick on the left is the one that was previously on our right because we're now looking at it from the other direction. So the stick on the left is the one that you claim the investigators wrongly measured and that's how they came up with an azimuth of 110 degrees. Now, you can also see the line marked north which is drawn here with an arrow and an N, and I take it you would agree that the left-hand stick makes an angle of less than 90 degrees with the direction north; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on a condition that what they marked as north is correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So if the investigators had measured this left-hand slat as you claim, they would not have come up with a direction of fire that was 110 degrees from north, would they? They would have come up with a direction of less than 90 degrees; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that I agree with this photo on a condition that they determined the north correctly. This north, I can't be sure that it is marked correctly. There is nothing to corroborate the correctness of this.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'd like you to assume for the purposes of my questions now that the investigators did -- were able to correctly identify the direction north. And you would also agree that the central axis, the stick marked with some red markings, the one that you agreed based on the previous photo accurately depicted the central axis, makes an angle a bit more than 90 degrees from north and would be consistent with the investigator's finding of 110 degrees; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is all correct on a condition that north is marked correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you. I'd like to move on now to incident G6 which is the 22nd of January, 1994, incident in Alipasino Polje where three mortar shells landed killing six children who had been playing in the snow and wounding another five persons. And this starts at paragraph 63 --

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Please, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: This is at page 45 in the English and 95 in the B/C/S. Now, what you were able to examine at the scene yourself was the remains of one of the three impacts because one of them at the time landed in soil and the other one landed on a surface that has since been repaved. And the remains of the crater that you were able to examine, apart from the deterioration of 17 years of wear and tear, it actually has been physically altered by repairs to the curb where the shell impacted; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to page 100 in the B/C/S where we can see figure 55 and this is at page 48 in the English and this relates to paragraph 67 of your report. And if we can zoom in on the photograph, please. Now, at paragraph 67 you claim that even though the curb has been repaired with concrete, when you went to the site in 2010 in your report you state: "It was quite obvious that the central crater is about 60 centimetres in diameter." And then you conclude that this is too large for an 82-millimetre shell. Now, I'm going to suggest to you that there are several factors that impact the reliability of your measurements. The first and most obvious is the repairs to the curb, which means you can really only see with any clarity one part of what remains of the crater. Secondly, the crater has obviously eroded over time which would be likely to make the crater larger as the erosion takes place. And since there have been repairs to the curb, it's quite likely that the crater itself was enlarged or manipulated by the people repairing it so that they could fill it in with concrete. Now, I'm going to suggest to you that those three factors render your measurement of at least 60 centimetres in 2010 totally unreliable and meaningless.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can absolutely not agree with you for the following reasons: First of all, it was not that the crater was repaired. An asphalt cube was placed on that or a concrete tube. The borders of the crater were not tampered with. Irrespective of the fact whether that crater was 60 or 55 and it was not smaller than that, if you look at its shape and if you look at figure 54, you can see that the fragmentation pattern was over 3 metres wide because that street was 6 metres wide. So this absolutely could not be the result of an 82-millimetre round. I suppose that we all know that. And another thing that I would like to indicate at this point is that Captain Verdy investigated on that day and he concluded that it was a detonation -- the detonation of a 120-millimetre round. I'm afraid that we were not the only ones who claimed that and also Captain Verdy was a very experienced investigator who --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm going to interrupt you because this is not what I asked you about. I asked you about the reliability of your measurement. We'll get into Mr. Verdy's calculations in a moment. Now, you just said that -- you made some assertions about the repairs to the curb. And you said: "The borders of the crater were not tampered with." But you didn't conduct any investigation into how this --

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You can see this in the image.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Wait for my question, please. You didn't conduct any investigation into how these repairs were conducted. You have no idea whether the people who repaired with this curb tampered with the crater or not. For example, you have no idea whether they cleaned out the crater in order to have a smoother surface in order to refill it. You can't draw any conclusions about what happened during the repairs because you weren't there and you didn't look into how the repairs were conducted; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is correct. However, there is another figure of that same crater on a different side of the street, and it is visible in the previous photo and it tallies with what we say about the crater. I'm saying that the measurements are reliable based on the traces that are still visible because there are additional traces arising from fragmentation and they are visible halfway through the street and it is impossible that they were created by an 82-millimetre round. This part of the crater in my view is very well preserved and despite all of your remarks it can well be used for the assessment of the type of mine that detonated in that street.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Again, Ms. Subotic, I'd like you to try to keep your answers concise and specifically directed to the question that I'm asking. Now --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I, please. The questions are regularly longer than the answers. The questions are longer than the answers. With all due respect, Ms. Gustafson, it is not fair on the witness to ask her to just answer by yes or no after questions that run over two pages of transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Subotic, at paragraph 68 - I'd like to move on to paragraph 68 now, which is at page 49 of the English and page 102 of the B/C/S - you -- if we could zoom in on this photo. In paragraph 68 you claim that Mr. Sabljica contradicted himself in his testimony. You state that although Mr. Sabljica initially stated that this -- the shell that made this impact came in from a direction slightly north of west, you say that he later agreed that the direction shown by the measuring tape on this photograph was properly established. And you repeated this in your testimony at transcript page 38262. Now, you were present when Mr. Sabljica testified so you must know that Mr. Sabljica, in fact, made it very clear that it was improper to establish direction of fire from a photograph and that this is not what they did at the time, and that's at transcript page 7829-7830 and when he was asked to draw the traces on this photo, he said: "Well, that's what we can see in the photo, at least." And that's T.7847 and D755. And when he was asked to mark fragments on another photo of this crater he said: "Yes, I will, but I have to stress again that a photo is not really the appropriate way to determine these things but here it is." That's T.7849 and D756. So when you claim in your report that Mr. Sabljica agreed that the direction shown by this measuring tape was properly established you're essentially misrepresenting his evidence because he made it quite clear that you could not properly establish anything on the basis of a photograph; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Sabljica in my view agreed with us and said that this is the fact that traces are well determined on the asphalt and that he established the trajectory of the shell correctly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. So you're aware, obviously, of the caveats he placed on the ability of -- to do these determinations through photographs, but you didn't consider that it was necessary to mention any of those caveats in your report when you said he agreed with what you've -- where you've placed the measuring tape here; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is not correct, please. These measurements were not based on the photo. The measurements were taken on site and then photos were taken. What you see here is not based on photos. This was done on site, but we then put it in a document in order to be able to include it in our findings. Measurements are not based on photos. Photos were taken of what it did, and Mr. Sabljica said as follows: He said that based on a photo he cannot agree to any degree of reliability. He didn't say that the measurements were wrongly taken because they were taken from a photo. Did you understand me now?

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I understand you, but what Mr. Sabljica was shown in court was a photograph and as you state he said that based on a photo he cannot agree to any degree of reliability. So in your report you said that he agreed with your measurement and you didn't think you needed to mention that he caveated that by saying that photos -- that these things can't be done on photos with any degree of reliability which is what he was being asked to do at the time; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It seems that the two of us are talking at cross-purposes. We don't understand each other. He said that his view, his assessment, cannot be exact because he is looking at a photo. Measurements were taken and depicted in a photo, so he is not questioning the way measurements were taken. He only said that he cannot state his opinion with any degree of reliability based on the photo alone, if this is -- you're correct that you're quoting him in this way. He said, As much as I can glean from a photo, that would be that. He's not questioning the way the original measurements were taken. Any one of us would react in the same way.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to page 109 of the B/C/S and figure 63, and this is paragraph 71 of your report and in English it's at page 53. And this is where you discuss Mr. -- the azimuths that Mr. Verdy measured and the conclusions that you draw from that. And your conclusion is that Mr. Verdy recorded the measurements backwards; in other words, he assigned -- he did the measurements but then assigned the measurements to the wrong shells -- wrong crater, sorry. And then when -- and then you've switched the measurements and then you conclude the azimuths meet at the UPI institute and the shells must have been fired from ABiH-held territory. And you -- the basis for this claim is, first, you claim that all three shells must have been fired from the same mortar; and then the shells must therefore have been fired from the point where the azimuths of the two impacts meet; and then you note that the azimuths recorded by Verdy do not meet, they actually diverge, because he recorded a slightly more northerly direction for the northern -- the impact that was more northerly and a bit more southerly direction for the southerly impact, so they don't meet in a point, they diverge. And so you've concluded that he made a mistake and you switched his calculations around to the opposite craters. Is that a correct summary of your position here?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to say something else, but the only thing I can say is that this is taken out of the context. First and foremost, we are not talking just about the co-ordinates that were determined by Captain Verdy. We're actually talking about azimuth angles. In our previous part of the text and in our previous discussion, we measured them on the materials that we had and our azimuths differ by only a few degrees in both places, and Mr. Verdy actually measured on the day when it happened, and to show respect for that we continued to use his measurements. Second of all, we noticed that Mr. Verdy switched the azimuths on the site but it was not us who then switched them back without checking first. The way he wrote down the physical evidence on the ground do not correspond to the trajectories. If they are noted in the way that Captain Verdy recorded them, then the physical evidence of the projectile impact on the ground do not tally with the trajectories that are marked. That was the reason why we noticed his mistake and corrected it accordingly. According to the range and the dissipation of fragments, we determined that they were fired from the same barrel and this was corroborated by Mr. Higgs and the investigators before us. It is not a novelty that we introduced to the table. And from those conclusions which were as follows, the measured and double-checked azimuths matched with the traces on the ground and the conclusion that they were fired from the same barrel based on the deviation - and that was established even before us - and based on all that, those two azimuths have to meet because the projectiles were fired from the same barrel and that is how we ended with the range that is stated in figure 62. So this is a fact, that's how things were. It is not us who concluded that without any foundation and without any checks of the kind that I have just explained to you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Does the Chamber wish to take a break now?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. We'll resume at 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before we continue -- yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Harvey.

utterances.speaker: MR. HARVEY
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours. Thank you. If I may just take this opportunity to introduce Mr. Aleksejs Babics, who has been working on my team for many months now and is from New York, or originally from Latvia, is qualified in the New York bar and is doing a masters degree at the University of Utrecht. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Ms. Subotic, do you have any problem with your headphones? Do you hear me?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My headphones don't seem to be working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Check the connection. That has been always my problem. Now do you hear me, Ms. Subotic? Otherwise we can replace your headphones with a proper one. So do you hear me now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's very soft.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I take it it now has been resolved?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there any further update as to the hearing next week or today? I've been told by the interpreters that they are having a workshop at 3.00, so we cannot go further than 3.00 today. So probably we can reduce the lunch break to half an hour and thereby having a half an hour extension for today. But for next week, is there any update?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Well, we discussed it at the break, trying to reach a mutual accommodation that involves the least disruption to the court schedule. I would say we made progress, but because we were unable to communicate until shortly before the session began I -- we weren't able to complete it. We'll keep working on it at the lunch break, however long that is, and see if we can't present to the Court a final schedule that everyone agrees with and that, as I say, hopefully involves the least disruption to the court personnel and the least burden.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Although it has not been finalised, it seems possible with the kind understanding and co-operation from the interpreters and other technical personnel that we sit an additional session for three days next week, i.e., for example, from 9.00 to 5.00, meaning for six hours a day. But I'm not sure it would be able to solve the -- all the problems in terms of scheduling. And the Chamber has in mind allowing the Prosecution around three and a half hours for the cross-examination of Mr. Lukic. So I'd like to hear more in detail after the lunch break.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We'll keep those -- that information in mind. Very helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, please continue, Ms. Gustafson.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Subotic, just before the break we were discussing your conclusions that Captain Verdy made a mistake --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt you. I have problem. I forgot to mention for record that we are sitting today pursuant to Rule 15 bis, with Judge Morrison being away due to his urgent matters. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And you stated that your conclusion about Captain Verdy's mistake was based on the physical evidence. You said that the physical evidence on the ground did not correspond to the trajectories. Now, yesterday when I asked you about the central axis method you made clear that the margin of error for the central axis method is at least plus/minus 5 degrees, you said plus/minus 5 to 10 degrees depending on the traces on the ground, and that's at transcript page 38359 and 38360. Now, the two azimuths that Mr. Verdy recorded, and this is at P1439, page 7, for the two craters were 4200 mils and 4.250 mils. And in the NATO system that corresponds to 236 degrees and 239 degrees. And the azimuths you measured based on the evidence available to you were 238 degrees and 240 degrees. And that's at paragraphs 68 and 70 in your report. So all of these measurements of the two craters are within 4 degrees of each other, between 236 and 240 degrees. So given that these four numbers are all within the minimum margin of error, well within the minimum margin of error, that you stated applied to the central axis method, you're not able to conclude that Mr. Verdy made a make because the measurements you've taken all fall well within the range of error of his measurements for either impact location; right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Translation, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was translated in Serbian whether that it cannot conclude that -- so what was translated into Serbian was that it cannot be concluded whether he did something, whereas it should have been that he did something. So -- of course the English is all right, but the interpretation reaching Ms. Subotic was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Your Honours, some of these corrections are becoming so minor that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Shall we put the question again, just the -- having heard all the -- all of your question, just simply put your question again then.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Subotic, you can't conclude that Mr. Verdy made any mistake in his calculations because -- for either of the two craters because your calculations fall well within the margin of error for either impact; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You would be right had the two projectiles landed on the same spot; however, they landed on two different spots which have different orientation relative to the north. And that's what causes the phenomenon that I refer to. If you invert the angles and place them the way he said on the spots that he marked, you will get the traces that are inverse not because of the deviation from the azimuth but because of the deviation in the positioning of the site relative to the north. Do you understand? The picture that will be shown on the point of impact, regardless of the fact that the trajectory has such a marginal difference, you would be right in what you are saying had they landed right next to each other, but they landed at two different positions in -- relative to the north. And because of the orientation of their impact and the place of impact, the traces indicate a different picture of the event than had been indicated in this finding.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript. [Interpretation] Line 17, what is missing in the transcript that one landed 200 metres away from the other.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: But, Ms. Subotic, the measurements you took are angle measurements, trajectory measurements, and both of your measurements fall well within the plus/minus 5-degree margin of error for both of his measurements. So wherever the impacts were in relation to each other doesn't detract from the fact that your -- either of your measurements have confirmed either of his measurements and you can't conclude that he got them backwards; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Have you completed your question? I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Again, not the entire question was interpreted, and this is a problem.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If you check the angles determined by Captain Verdy in the locations as marked by him, regardless of the difference that exists between the two and whether it is within the margin of error, if they are taken and the fact of the matter is that the projectiles were fired from the same weapon, then their trajectories when plotted this way will intersect at a site that is completely different to the one indicated by the physical trace retrieved in the field, in the area where they were active. The intersection would, in fact, be at a side that is completely opposite to this one.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Subotic, the last part of -- the very last thing you said was not interpreted. Could you just repeat the last few words that you spoke.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said that if the lines of azimuth are drawn from the firing points of both of these projectiles, these lines will intersect at a side that is quite the opposite to the lines as indicated by the physical evidence on the asphalt. It has to be compatible. Do you understand? And it was on this basis that it was determined and not on the basis of the accuracy of the measurements.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: The Prosecutor is kindly asked to allow some time for the interpretation. That has been the reason for interventions with regard to the interpretation. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I apologise. I will speak more slowly.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Ms. Subotic, we're now back at your assertion that the two azimuths must meet at a single point, so I'd like to show you 65 ter 24520. And while that's coming up, again I'm going to suggest to you that your assertion that the two azimuths recorded by Mr. Verdy must meet at a single point is a flawed one because it doesn't take into account the margin of error of at least plus/minus 5 degrees. And the map that should be coming up on your screen in a moment is a map that depicts the two azimuths recorded by Mr. Verdy with a plus/minus 5-degree margin of error. And the map shows that when you take into account an appropriate margin of error, there is a large area of territory that's depicted in the -- with the darker yellow on this map from which the shells could be fired. Now, you agree that when you take into account an appropriate margin of error, it's clear that you cannot assert that the azimuths of the two impacts must meet at a single point; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We could make an analysis which would provide these intersections or convergence points. At any rate, the azimuth from two angles standing for the firing points from the same barrel must converge in a single point, regardless of what we have to say about the accuracy of the method of measurement. If the projectiles are fired from a single weapon, then the azimuths for each of the rounds fired must converge in a single point. Regardless of how many projectiles are fired from a single barrel and regardless of how different the azimuths are, they must converge in a single point. It's one of the characteristics of the weapon, regardless of the method of measurement applied.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay, Ms. Subotic, even assuming you're correct in this case that these shells were fired from a single barrel, the point is that the barrel could have been anywhere in the dark yellow cone you see here, and that would be consistent with what Captain Verdy measured when you take into account the appropriate margin of error for those measurements; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. Allow me, please. What we're talking about here is the determination of the distance, not of the azimuth. What is marked in yellow and darker yellow, you can see that it is all converging in one point. All these angles are converging in this point. Can you see that? We're talking about the distance, not about the angle. Both the lighter and the darker yellow and the lighter yellow above is the range of the accuracy of measurement. But if you have a look at it, you will see that they all converge in one point up there. And that's what I'm telling you, they have to intersect in a single point. As I told you a moment ago, all the projectiles, regardless of the azimuth, if fired from the same weapon, from the same barrel must converge and intersect in a single point. This has nothing to do with the measurement. Do you see? The area that you marked covers the accuracy of measurement of the azimuths that we have covered here. And I do agree with you that this is the accuracy of the measurement of the azimuth. However, what we're talking about is the distance that is determined. You see that both the left-most and the right-most and the central lines are all converging in one point up there because that is one of the characteristics of the weapon, of the system, regardless of the method of measurement. You see, we're talking about a specific distance as determined by the trajectories ending in a certain point. I don't know how clear I was.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: It's, frankly, not clear to me. Are you saying that because it's your position that these shells were fired from the same barrel that Captain Verdy must have made a mistake? Does this depend on your assertion that the shells were fired from the same mortar barrel?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. Please. Captain Verdy measured certain azimuths and defined them or tied them in with certain points -- firing points. We checked his measurement and we obtained a result that was a match but an inverse one. This was the first parameter on the basis of which we were able to see that there was an error there. Thirdly, the investigators before us as well as we on the basis of the characteristics of the systems -- of the system established that it was the same barrel. This was a finding by Mr. Higgs as well. So this is not just an assumption. On the basis of the evidence found on the asphalt and on the basis of the checks we did, we concluded, above all, that Captain Verdy must have confused numerical values, must have mistaken them. But they were so marginal that we didn't want to pay much attention to them. But on the basis of the overall evidence on the asphalt and the result of this explosion that we were able to see from the documentation and on the site itself, we concluded that there was an error. And as we know, even before we analysed this, it was established that they were fired from the same barrel and it was on this basis that we produced the picture that we did, and on the basis of that picture we were able to gauge the distance. The way he wrote it, these lines would intersect at a side that will be quite a different one and that would not be consistent with the physical evidence.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'm going to -- thank you. I'm going to move on to G7. This is the 4th of February, 1993, incident, where three 120-millimetre mortar shells landed in an area of Dobrinja.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Sorry.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: And the discussion of this begins at page 59 of the English and page 114 of the B/C/S. Now, just as a preliminary matter, there are no remains left of any of these craters, so in your own analysis you were not able to examine in person any of the craters themselves; right?

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We attended the scene and what we found there was that the surface on which the shell on Mihajla Pupina Street impacted was changed as was the case on the playground. We based our findings on the documents produced by the CSB and the remaining physical evidence of fragmentation that remained intact as compared to the situation that prevailed at the time. And we documented this by photographing the scene when we visited it.

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. If we could go to page 120 in the B/C/S, and this is paragraph 80 of your report and the English page reference is page 62. And if we could zoom in on the photograph and maybe collapse the English. Now, you have a theory about how there were actually four shells fired in this incident rather than three, and one of the reasons you reached that conclusion is that in your view this photograph depicts in the yellow circle damage that could not have been caused by the shell exploding on the footpath marked with the number 1 here but only from the shrapnel of a shell that exploded on the playground. And if we could just zoom in on what's in the yellow circle. Now, Ms. Subotic - that's fine, this is perfect - if you could just with a pen trace precisely what you consider to be the shrapnel damage that could not have been caused by the shell that hit the footpath.

utterances.speaker: ZORICA SUBOTIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Marks]

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. If you could just --

utterances.speaker: MS. GUSTAFSON
utterances.text: I'd just like to tender that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Could you put the date and your initial on the upper part. For record, you put number 1 for the marking.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have already made the marking, number 1.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I noted for record. Yes. We'll admit it as Prosecution Exhibit.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
